## comando ```sh cd /home/one/projects/one/ai-guides/frameworks/laravel13_guide && nl -ba samples/doc-logging.md ``` ## resultado 1 # Logging 2 3 - [Introduction](#introduction) 4 - [Configuration](#configuration) 5 - [Available Channel Drivers](#available-channel-drivers) 6 - [Channel Prerequisites](#channel-prerequisites) 7 - [Logging Deprecation Warnings](#logging-deprecation-warnings) 8 - [Building Log Stacks](#building-log-stacks) 9 - [Writing Log Messages](#writing-log-messages) 10 - [Contextual Information](#contextual-information) 11 - [Writing to Specific Channels](#writing-to-specific-channels) 12 - [Monolog Channel Customization](#monolog-channel-customization) 13 - [Customizing Monolog for Channels](#customizing-monolog-for-channels) 14 - [Creating Monolog Handler Channels](#creating-monolog-handler-channels) 15 - [Creating Custom Channels via Factories](#creating-custom-channels-via-factories) 16 - [Tailing Log Messages Using Pail](#tailing-log-messages-using-pail) 17 - [Installation](#pail-installation) 18 - [Usage](#pail-usage) 19 - [Filtering Logs](#pail-filtering-logs) 20 21 22 ## Introduction 23 24 To help you learn more about what's happening within your application, Laravel provides robust logging services that allow you to log messages to files, the system error log, and even to Slack to notify your entire team. 25 26 Laravel logging is based on "channels". Each channel represents a specific way of writing log information. For example, the `single` channel writes log files to a single log file, while the `slack` channel sends log messages to Slack. Log messages may be written to multiple channels based on their severity. 27 28 Under the hood, Laravel utilizes the [Monolog](https://github.com/Seldaek/monolog) library, which provides support for a variety of powerful log handlers. Laravel makes it a cinch to configure these handlers, allowing you to mix and match them to customize your application's log handling. 29 30 31 ## Configuration 32 33 All of the configuration options that control your application's logging behavior are housed in the `config/logging.php` configuration file. This file allows you to configure your application's log channels, so be sure to review each of the available channels and their options. We'll review a few common options below. 34 35 By default, Laravel will use the `stack` channel when logging messages. The `stack` channel is used to aggregate multiple log channels into a single channel. For more information on building stacks, check out the [documentation below](#building-log-stacks). 36 37 38 ### Available Channel Drivers 39 40 Each log channel is powered by a "driver". The driver determines how and where the log message is actually recorded. The following log channel drivers are available in every Laravel application. An entry for most of these drivers is already present in your application's `config/logging.php` configuration file, so be sure to review this file to become familiar with its contents: 41 42
43 44 | Name | Description | 45 | ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | 46 | `custom` | A driver that calls a specified factory to create a channel. | 47 | `daily` | A `RotatingFileHandler` based Monolog driver which rotates daily. | 48 | `monthly` | A `RotatingFileHandler` based Monolog driver which rotates monthly. | 49 | `errorlog` | An `ErrorLogHandler` based Monolog driver. | 50 | `monolog` | A Monolog factory driver that may use any supported Monolog handler. | 51 | `single` | A single file or path based logger channel (`StreamHandler`). | 52 | `slack` | A `SlackWebhookHandler` based Monolog driver. | 53 | `stack` | A wrapper to facilitate creating "multi-channel" channels. | 54 | `syslog` | A `SyslogHandler` based Monolog driver. | 55 56
57 58 > [!NOTE] 59 > Check out the documentation on [advanced channel customization](#monolog-channel-customization) to learn more about the `monolog` and `custom` drivers. 60 61 62 #### Configuring the Channel Name 63 64 By default, Monolog is instantiated with a "channel name" that matches the current environment, such as `production` or `local`. To change this value, you may add a `name` option to your channel's configuration: 65 66 ```php 67 'stack' => [ 68 'driver' => 'stack', 69 'name' => 'channel-name', 70 'channels' => ['single', 'slack'], 71 ], 72 ``` 73 74 75 ### Channel Prerequisites 76 77 78 #### Configuring the Single, Daily, and Monthly Channels 79 80 The `single`, `daily`, and `monthly` channels have three optional configuration options: `bubble`, `permission`, and `locking`. 81 82
83 84 | Name | Description | Default | 85 | ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | 86 | `bubble` | Indicates if messages should bubble up to other channels after being handled. | `true` | 87 | `locking` | Attempt to lock the log file before writing to it. | `false` | 88 | `permission` | The log file's permissions. | `0644` | 89 90
91 92 Additionally, the retention policy for the `daily` and `monthly` channels can be configured via the `max_files` configuration option. The `LOG_DAILY_DAYS` environment variable may also be used to configure retention for the `daily` channel. 93 94 95 #### Configuring the Papertrail Channel 96 97 The `papertrail` channel requires `host` and `port` configuration options. These may be defined via the `PAPERTRAIL_URL` and `PAPERTRAIL_PORT` environment variables. You can obtain these values from [Papertrail](https://help.papertrailapp.com/kb/configuration/configuring-centralized-logging-from-php-apps/#send-events-from-php-app). 98 99 100 #### Configuring the Slack Channel 101 102 The `slack` channel requires a `url` configuration option. This value may be defined via the `LOG_SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL` environment variable. This URL should match a URL for an [incoming webhook](https://slack.com/apps/A0F7XDUAZ-incoming-webhooks) that you have configured for your Slack team. 103 104 By default, Slack will only receive logs at the `critical` level and above; however, you can adjust this using the `LOG_LEVEL` environment variable or by modifying the `level` configuration option within your Slack log channel's configuration array. 105 106 107 ### Logging Deprecation Warnings 108 109 PHP, Laravel, and other libraries often notify their users that some of their features have been deprecated and will be removed in a future version. If you would like to log these deprecation warnings, you may specify your preferred `deprecations` log channel using the `LOG_DEPRECATIONS_CHANNEL` environment variable, or within your application's `config/logging.php` configuration file: 110 111 ```php 112 'deprecations' => [ 113 'channel' => env('LOG_DEPRECATIONS_CHANNEL', 'null'), 114 'trace' => env('LOG_DEPRECATIONS_TRACE', false), 115 ], 116 117 'channels' => [ 118 // ... 119 ] 120 ``` 121 122 Or, you may define a log channel named `deprecations`. If a log channel with this name exists, it will always be used to log deprecations: 123 124 ```php 125 'channels' => [ 126 'deprecations' => [ 127 'driver' => 'single', 128 'path' => storage_path('logs/php-deprecation-warnings.log'), 129 ], 130 ], 131 ``` 132 133 134 ## Building Log Stacks 135 136 As mentioned previously, the `stack` driver allows you to combine multiple channels into a single log channel for convenience. To illustrate how to use log stacks, let's take a look at an example configuration that you might see in a production application: 137 138 ```php 139 'channels' => [ 140 'stack' => [ 141 'driver' => 'stack', 142 'channels' => ['syslog', 'slack'], // [tl! add] 143 'ignore_exceptions' => false, 144 ], 145 146 'syslog' => [ 147 'driver' => 'syslog', 148 'level' => env('LOG_LEVEL', 'debug'), 149 'facility' => env('LOG_SYSLOG_FACILITY', LOG_USER), 150 'replace_placeholders' => true, 151 ], 152 153 'slack' => [ 154 'driver' => 'slack', 155 'url' => env('LOG_SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL'), 156 'username' => env('LOG_SLACK_USERNAME', 'Laravel Log'), 157 'emoji' => env('LOG_SLACK_EMOJI', ':boom:'), 158 'level' => env('LOG_LEVEL', 'critical'), 159 'replace_placeholders' => true, 160 ], 161 ], 162 ``` 163 164 Let's dissect this configuration. First, notice our `stack` channel aggregates two other channels via its `channels` option: `syslog` and `slack`. So, when logging messages, both of these channels will have the opportunity to log the message. However, as we will see below, whether these channels actually log the message may be determined by the message's severity / "level". 165 166 167 #### Log Levels 168 169 Take note of the `level` configuration option present on the `syslog` and `slack` channel configurations in the example above. This option determines the minimum "level" a message must be in order to be logged by the channel. Monolog, which powers Laravel's logging services, offers all of the log levels defined in the [RFC 5424 specification](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5424). In descending order of severity, these log levels are: **emergency**, **alert**, **critical**, **error**, **warning**, **notice**, **info**, and **debug**. 170 171 So, imagine we log a message using the `debug` method: 172 173 ```php 174 Log::debug('An informational message.'); 175 ``` 176 177 Given our configuration, the `syslog` channel will write the message to the system log; however, since the error message is not `critical` or above, it will not be sent to Slack. However, if we log an `emergency` message, it will be sent to both the system log and Slack since the `emergency` level is above our minimum level threshold for both channels: 178 179 ```php 180 Log::emergency('The system is down!'); 181 ``` 182 183 184 ## Writing Log Messages 185 186 You may write information to the logs using the `Log` [facade](/docs/{{version}}/facades). As previously mentioned, the logger provides the eight logging levels defined in the [RFC 5424 specification](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5424): **emergency**, **alert**, **critical**, **error**, **warning**, **notice**, **info** and **debug**: 187 188 ```php 189 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Log; 190 191 Log::emergency($message); 192 Log::alert($message); 193 Log::critical($message); 194 Log::error($message); 195 Log::warning($message); 196 Log::notice($message); 197 Log::info($message); 198 Log::debug($message); 199 ``` 200 201 You may call any of these methods to log a message for the corresponding level. By default, the message will be written to the default log channel as configured by your `logging` configuration file: 202 203 ```php 204 $id]); 220 221 return view('user.profile', [ 222 'user' => User::findOrFail($id) 223 ]); 224 } 225 } 226 ``` 227 228 229 ### Contextual Information 230 231 An array of contextual data may be passed to the log methods. This contextual data will be formatted and displayed with the log message: 232 233 ```php 234 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Log; 235 236 Log::info('User {id} failed to login.', ['id' => $user->id]); 237 ``` 238 239 Occasionally, you may wish to specify some contextual information that should be included with all subsequent log entries in a particular channel. For example, you may wish to log a request ID that is associated with each incoming request to your application. To accomplish this, you may call the `Log` facade's `withContext` method: 240 241 ```php 242 $requestId 265 ]); 266 267 $response = $next($request); 268 269 $response->headers->set('Request-Id', $requestId); 270 271 return $response; 272 } 273 } 274 ``` 275 276 If you would like to share contextual information across _all_ logging channels, you may invoke the `Log::shareContext()` method. This method will provide the contextual information to all created channels and any channels that are created subsequently: 277 278 ```php 279 $requestId 302 ]); 303 304 // ... 305 } 306 } 307 ``` 308 309 > [!NOTE] 310 > If you need to share log context while processing queued jobs, you may utilize [job middleware](/docs/{{version}}/queues#job-middleware). 311 312 313 ### Writing to Specific Channels 314 315 Sometimes you may wish to log a message to a channel other than your application's default channel. You may use the `channel` method on the `Log` facade to retrieve and log to any channel defined in your configuration file: 316 317 ```php 318 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Log; 319 320 Log::channel('slack')->info('Something happened!'); 321 ``` 322 323 If you would like to create an on-demand logging stack consisting of multiple channels, you may use the `stack` method: 324 325 ```php 326 Log::stack(['single', 'slack'])->info('Something happened!'); 327 ``` 328 329 330 #### On-Demand Channels 331 332 It is also possible to create an on-demand channel by providing the configuration at runtime without that configuration being present in your application's `logging` configuration file. To accomplish this, you may pass a configuration array to the `Log` facade's `build` method: 333 334 ```php 335 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Log; 336 337 Log::build([ 338 'driver' => 'single', 339 'path' => storage_path('logs/custom.log'), 340 ])->info('Something happened!'); 341 ``` 342 343 You may also wish to include an on-demand channel in an on-demand logging stack. This can be achieved by including your on-demand channel instance in the array passed to the `stack` method: 344 345 ```php 346 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Log; 347 348 $channel = Log::build([ 349 'driver' => 'single', 350 'path' => storage_path('logs/custom.log'), 351 ]); 352 353 Log::stack(['slack', $channel])->info('Something happened!'); 354 ``` 355 356 357 ## Monolog Channel Customization 358 359 360 ### Customizing Monolog for Channels 361 362 Sometimes you may need complete control over how Monolog is configured for an existing channel. For example, you may want to configure a custom Monolog `FormatterInterface` implementation for Laravel's built-in `single` channel. 363 364 To get started, define a `tap` array on the channel's configuration. The `tap` array should contain a list of classes that should have an opportunity to customize (or "tap" into) the Monolog instance after it is created. There is no conventional location where these classes should be placed, so you are free to create a directory within your application to contain these classes: 365 366 ```php 367 'single' => [ 368 'driver' => 'single', 369 'tap' => [App\Logging\CustomizeFormatter::class], 370 'path' => storage_path('logs/laravel.log'), 371 'level' => env('LOG_LEVEL', 'debug'), 372 'replace_placeholders' => true, 373 ], 374 ``` 375 376 Once you have configured the `tap` option on your channel, you're ready to define the class that will customize your Monolog instance. This class only needs a single method: `__invoke`, which receives an `Illuminate\Log\Logger` instance. The `Illuminate\Log\Logger` instance proxies all method calls to the underlying Monolog instance: 377 378 ```php 379 getHandlers() as $handler) { 394 $handler->setFormatter(new LineFormatter( 395 '[%datetime%] %channel%.%level_name%: %message% %context% %extra%' 396 …

## comando ```sh cd /home/one/projects/one/ai-guides/frameworks/laravel13_guide && nl -ba samples/doc-context.md ``` ## resultado 1 # Context 2 3 - [Introduction](#introduction) 4 - [How it Works](#how-it-works) 5 - [Capturing Context](#capturing-context) 6 - [Stacks](#stacks) 7 - [Retrieving Context](#retrieving-context) 8 - [Determining Item Existence](#determining-item-existence) 9 - [Removing Context](#removing-context) 10 - [Hidden Context](#hidden-context) 11 - [Events](#events) 12 - [Dehydrating](#dehydrating) 13 - [Hydrated](#hydrated) 14 15 16 ## Introduction 17 18 Laravel's "context" capabilities enable you to capture, retrieve, and share information throughout requests, jobs, and commands executing within your application. This captured information is also included in logs written by your application, giving you deeper insight into the surrounding code execution history that occurred before a log entry was written and allowing you to trace execution flows throughout a distributed system. 19 20 21 ### How it Works 22 23 The best way to understand Laravel's context capabilities is to see it in action using the built-in logging features. To get started, you may [add information to the context](#capturing-context) using the `Context` facade. In this example, we will use a [middleware](/docs/{{version}}/middleware) to add the request URL and a unique trace ID to the context on every incoming request: 24 25 ```php 26 url()); 44 Context::add('trace_id', Str::uuid()->toString()); 45 46 return $next($request); 47 } 48 } 49 ``` 50 51 Information added to the context is automatically appended as metadata to any [log entries](/docs/{{version}}/logging) that are written throughout the request. Appending context as metadata allows information passed to individual log entries to be differentiated from the information shared via `Context`. For example, imagine we write the following log entry: 52 53 ```php 54 Log::info('User authenticated.', ['auth_id' => Auth::id()]); 55 ``` 56 57 The written log will contain the `auth_id` passed to the log entry, but it will also contain the context's `url` and `trace_id` as metadata: 58 59 ```text 60 User authenticated. {"auth_id":27} {"url":"https://example.com/login","trace_id":"e04e1a11-e75c-4db3-b5b5-cfef4ef56697"} 61 ``` 62 63 Information added to the context is also made available to jobs dispatched to the queue. For example, imagine we dispatch a `ProcessPodcast` job to the queue after adding some information to the context: 64 65 ```php 66 // In our middleware... 67 Context::add('url', $request->url()); 68 Context::add('trace_id', Str::uuid()->toString()); 69 70 // In our controller... 71 ProcessPodcast::dispatch($podcast); 72 ``` 73 74 When the job is dispatched, any information currently stored in the context is captured and shared with the job. The captured information is then hydrated back into the current context while the job is executing. So, if our job's handle method was to write to the log: 75 76 ```php 77 class ProcessPodcast implements ShouldQueue 78 { 79 use Queueable; 80 81 // ... 82 83 /** 84 * Execute the job. 85 */ 86 public function handle(): void 87 { 88 Log::info('Processing podcast.', [ 89 'podcast_id' => $this->podcast->id, 90 ]); 91 92 // ... 93 } 94 } 95 ``` 96 97 The resulting log entry would contain the information that was added to the context during the request that originally dispatched the job: 98 99 ```text 100 Processing podcast. {"podcast_id":95} {"url":"https://example.com/login","trace_id":"e04e1a11-e75c-4db3-b5b5-cfef4ef56697"} 101 ``` 102 103 Although we have focused on the built-in logging related features of Laravel's context, the following documentation will illustrate how context allows you to share information across the HTTP request / queued job boundary and even how to add [hidden context data](#hidden-context) that is not written with log entries. 104 105 106 ## Capturing Context 107 108 You may store information in the current context using the `Context` facade's `add` method: 109 110 ```php 111 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Context; 112 113 Context::add('key', 'value'); 114 ``` 115 116 To add multiple items at once, you may pass an associative array to the `add` method: 117 118 ```php 119 Context::add([ 120 'first_key' => 'value', 121 'second_key' => 'value', 122 ]); 123 ``` 124 125 The `add` method will override any existing value that shares the same key. If you only wish to add information to the context if the key does not already exist, you may use the `addIf` method: 126 127 ```php 128 Context::add('key', 'first'); 129 130 Context::get('key'); 131 // "first" 132 133 Context::addIf('key', 'second'); 134 135 Context::get('key'); 136 // "first" 137 ``` 138 139 Context also provides convenient methods for incrementing or decrementing a given key. Both of these methods accept at least one argument: the key to track. A second argument may be provided to specify the amount by which the key should be incremented or decremented: 140 141 ```php 142 Context::increment('records_added'); 143 Context::increment('records_added', 5); 144 145 Context::decrement('records_added'); 146 Context::decrement('records_added', 5); 147 ``` 148 149 150 #### Conditional Context 151 152 The `when` method may be used to add data to the context based on a given condition. The first closure provided to the `when` method will be invoked if the given condition evaluates to `true`, while the second closure will be invoked if the condition evaluates to `false`: 153 154 ```php 155 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Auth; 156 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Context; 157 158 Context::when( 159 Auth::user()->isAdmin(), 160 fn ($context) => $context->add('permissions', Auth::user()->permissions), 161 fn ($context) => $context->add('permissions', []), 162 ); 163 ``` 164 165 166 #### Scoped Context 167 168 The `scope` method provides a way to temporarily modify the context during the execution of a given callback and restore the context to its original state when the callback finishes executing. Additionally, you can pass extra data that should be merged into the context (as the second and third arguments) while the closure executes. 169 170 ```php 171 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Context; 172 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Log; 173 174 Context::add('trace_id', 'abc-999'); 175 Context::addHidden('user_id', 123); 176 177 Context::scope( 178 function () { 179 Context::add('action', 'adding_friend'); 180 181 $userId = Context::getHidden('user_id'); 182 183 Log::debug("Adding user [{$userId}] to friends list."); 184 // Adding user [987] to friends list. {"trace_id":"abc-999","user_name":"taylor_otwell","action":"adding_friend"} 185 }, 186 data: ['user_name' => 'taylor_otwell'], 187 hidden: ['user_id' => 987], 188 ); 189 190 Context::all(); 191 // [ 192 // 'trace_id' => 'abc-999', 193 // ] 194 195 Context::allHidden(); 196 // [ 197 // 'user_id' => 123, 198 // ] 199 ``` 200 201 > [!WARNING] 202 > If an object within the context is modified inside the scoped closure, that mutation will be reflected outside of the scope. 203 204 205 ### Stacks 206 207 Context offers the ability to create "stacks", which are lists of data stored in the order that they were added. You can add information to a stack by invoking the `push` method: 208 209 ```php 210 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Context; 211 212 Context::push('breadcrumbs', 'first_value'); 213 214 Context::push('breadcrumbs', 'second_value', 'third_value'); 215 216 Context::get('breadcrumbs'); 217 // [ 218 // 'first_value', 219 // 'second_value', 220 // 'third_value', 221 // ] 222 ``` 223 224 Stacks can be useful to capture historical information about a request, such as events that are happening throughout your application. For example, you could create an event listener to push to a stack every time a query is executed, capturing the query SQL and duration as a tuple: 225 226 ```php 227 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Context; 228 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB; 229 230 // In AppServiceProvider.php... 231 DB::listen(function ($event) { 232 Context::push('queries', [$event->time, $event->sql]); 233 }); 234 ``` 235 236 You may determine if a value is in a stack using the `stackContains` and `hiddenStackContains` methods: 237 238 ```php 239 if (Context::stackContains('breadcrumbs', 'first_value')) { 240 // 241 } 242 243 if (Context::hiddenStackContains('secrets', 'first_value')) { 244 // 245 } 246 ``` 247 248 The `stackContains` and `hiddenStackContains` methods also accept a closure as their second argument, allowing more control over the value comparison operation: 249 250 ```php 251 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Context; 252 use Illuminate\Support\Str; 253 254 return Context::stackContains('breadcrumbs', function ($value) { 255 return Str::startsWith($value, 'query_'); 256 }); 257 ``` 258 259 260 ## Retrieving Context 261 262 You may retrieve information from the context using the `Context` facade's `get` method: 263 264 ```php 265 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Context; 266 267 $value = Context::get('key'); 268 ``` 269 270 The `only` and `except` methods may be used to retrieve a subset of the information in the context: 271 272 ```php 273 $data = Context::only(['first_key', 'second_key']); 274 275 $data = Context::except(['first_key']); 276 ``` 277 278 The `pull` method may be used to retrieve information from the context and immediately remove it from the context: 279 280 ```php 281 $value = Context::pull('key'); 282 ``` 283 284 If context data is stored in a [stack](#stacks), you may pop items from the stack using the `pop` method: 285 286 ```php 287 Context::push('breadcrumbs', 'first_value', 'second_value'); 288 289 Context::pop('breadcrumbs'); 290 // second_value 291 292 Context::get('breadcrumbs'); 293 // ['first_value'] 294 ``` 295 296 The `remember` and `rememberHidden` methods may be used to retrieve information from the context, while setting the context value to the value returned by the given closure if the requested information doesn't exist: 297 298 ```php 299 $permissions = Context::remember( 300 'user-permissions', 301 fn () => $user->permissions, 302 ); 303 ``` 304 305 If you would like to retrieve all of the information stored in the context, you may invoke the `all` method: 306 307 ```php 308 $data = Context::all(); 309 ``` 310 311 312 ### Determining Item Existence 313 314 You may use the `has` and `missing` methods to determine if the context has any value stored for the given key: 315 316 ```php 317 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Context; 318 319 if (Context::has('key')) { 320 // ... 321 } 322 323 if (Context::missing('key')) { 324 // ... 325 } 326 ``` 327 328 The `has` method will return `true` regardless of the value stored. So, for example, a key with a `null` value will be considered present: 329 330 ```php 331 Context::add('key', null); 332 333 Context::has('key'); 334 // true 335 ``` 336 337 338 ## Removing Context 339 340 The `forget` method may be used to remove a key and its value from the current context: 341 342 ```php 343 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Context; 344 345 Context::add(['first_key' => 1, 'second_key' => 2]); 346 347 Context::forget('first_key'); 348 349 Context::all(); 350 351 // ['second_key' => 2] 352 ``` 353 354 You may forget several keys at once by providing an array to the `forget` method: 355 356 ```php 357 Context::forget(['first_key', 'second_key']); 358 ``` 359 360 361 ## Hidden Context 362 363 Context offers the ability to store "hidden" data. This hidden information is not appended to logs, and is not accessible via the data retrieval methods documented above. Context provides a different set of methods to interact with hidden context information: 364 365 ```php 366 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Context; 367 368 Context::addHidden('key', 'value'); 369 370 Context::getHidden('key'); 371 // 'value' 372 373 Context::get('key'); 374 // null 375 ``` 376 377 The "hidden" methods mirror the functionality of the non-hidden methods documented above: 378 379 ```php 380 Context::addHidden(/* ... */); 381 Context::addHiddenIf(/* ... */); 382 Context::pushHidden(/* ... */); 383 Context::getHidden(/* ... */); 384 Context::pullHidden(/* ... */); 385 Context::popHidden(/* ... */); 386 Context::onlyHidden(/* ... */); 387 Context::exceptHidden(/* ... */); 388 Context::allHidden(/* ... */); 389 Context::hasHidden(/* ... */); 390 Context::missingHidden(/* ... */); 391 Context::forgetHidden(/* ... */); 392 ``` 393 394 395 ## Events 396 397 Context dispatches two events that allow you to hook into the hydration and dehydration process of the context. 398 399 To illustrate how these events may be used, imagine that in a middleware of your application you set the `app.locale` configuration value based on the incoming HTTP request's `Accept-Language` header. Context's events allow you to capture this value during the request and restore it on the queue, ensuring notifications sent on the queue have the correct `app.locale` value. We can use context's events and [hidden](#hidden-context) data to achieve this, which the following documentation will illustrate. 400 401 402 ### Dehydrating 403 404 Whenever a job is dispatched to the queue the data in the context is "dehydrated" and captured alongside the job's payload. The `Context::dehydrating` method allows you to register a closure that will be invoked during the dehydration process. Within this closure, you may make changes to the data that will be shared with the queued job. 405 406 Typically, you should register `dehydrating` callbacks within the `boot` method of your application's `AppServiceProvider` class: 407 408 ```php 409 use Illuminate\Log\Context\Repository; 410 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Config; 411 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Context; 412 413 /** 414 * Bootstrap any application services. 415 */ 416 public function boot(): void 417 { 418 Context::dehydrating(function (Repository $context) { 419 $context->addHidden('locale', Config::get('app.locale')); 420 }); 421 } 422 ``` 423 424 > [!NOTE] 425 > You should not use the `Context` facade within the `dehydrating` callback, as that will change the context of the current process. Ensure you only make changes to the repository passed to the callback. 426 427 428 ### Hydrated 429 430 Whenever a queued job begins executing on the queue, any context that was shared with the job will be "hydrated" back into the current context. The `Context::hydrated` method allows you to register a closure that will be invoked during the hydration process. 431 432 Typically, you should register `hydrated` callbacks within the `boot` method of your application's `AppServiceProvider` class: 433 434 ```php 435 use Illuminate\Log\Context\Repository; 436 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Config; 437 use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Context; 438 439 /** 440 * Bootstrap any application services. 441 */ 442 public function boot(): void 443 { 444 Context::hydrated(function (Repository $context) { 445 if ($context->hasHidden('locale')) { 446 Config::set('app.locale', $context->getHidden('locale')); 447 } 448 }); 449 } 450 ``` 451 452 > [!NOTE] 453 > You should not use the `Context` facade within the `hydrated` callback and instead ensure you only make changes to the repository passed to the callback.

# 1. `config/logging.php` completo (skeleton 13.x)

## 1.1 Topo e seleção de canal

**Canal padrão.** `samples/samples-config-logging.php:21`:
```php
'default' => env('LOG_CHANNEL', 'stack'),
```
O padrão é o `stack`, que a documentação define como agregador de múltiplos canais (`samples/doc-logging.md:35`). O valor precisa corresponder a um canal declarado em `channels` (`samples/samples-config-logging.php:15-17`).

**Drivers disponíveis.** O skeleton lista explicitamente (`samples/samples-config-logging.php:48-49`): `single`, `daily`, `monthly`, `slack`, `syslog`, `errorlog`, `monolog`, `custom`, `stack`. A tabela oficial (`samples/doc-logging.md:44-54`) mapeia: `custom` (factory), `daily`/`monthly` (`RotatingFileHandler`), `errorlog` (`ErrorLogHandler`), `monolog` (qualquer handler), `single` (`StreamHandler`), `slack` (`SlackWebhookHandler`), `stack` (multi-canal), `syslog` (`SyslogHandler`). A documentação recomenda rever o arquivo do próprio projeto porque a maioria dos drivers já vem presente (`samples/doc-logging.md:40`).

**Nome do canal Monolog.** Por padrão o nome segue o ambiente (`production`, `local`); a chave `name` o substitui (`samples/doc-logging.md:64`), com exemplo literali em `samples/doc-logging.md:66-72` — `'stack' => ['driver' => 'stack', 'name' => 'channel-name', 'channels' => ['single', 'slack']]`.

## 1.2 Deprecations

`samples/samples-config-logging.php:34-37`:
```php
'deprecations' => [
    'channel' => env('LOG_DEPRECATIONS_CHANNEL', 'null'),
    'trace' => env('LOG_DEPRECATIONS_TRACE', false),
],
```
O canal de deprecations pode ser escolhido por `LOG_DEPRECATIONS_CHANNEL` ou no próprio array; isso permite preparar o app para versões futuras de dependências (`samples/doc-logging.md:109`). O skeleton usa `null` como padrão (`samples/samples-config-logging.php:35`) — ou seja, **por padrão nada é registrado**; ativar exige apontar para `single`, `daily` etc. Há alternativa: declarar um canal chamado `deprecations`, que passa a ser **sempre** usado (`samples/doc-logging.md:122`), com exemplo literali em `samples/doc-logging.md:124-131`:
```php
'channels' => [
    'deprecations' => [
        'driver' => 'single',
        'path' => storage_path('logs/php-deprecation-warnings.log'),
    ],
],
```
O `trace` controla inclusão de stack trace (`samples/samples-config-logging.php:36`; variável `LOG_DEPRECATIONS_TRACE` em `samples/doc-logging.md:114`); a documentação lida não detalha o formato do traço — formato específico: **não verificado**.

## 1.3 Stacks e níveis

`samples/samples-config-logging.php:55-59`:
```php
'stack' => [
    'driver' => 'stack',
    'channels' => explode(',', (string) env('LOG_STACK', 'single')),
    'ignore_exceptions' => false,
],
```
`LOG_STACK` é uma lista separada por vírgula; padrão `single`. `ignore_exceptions => false` está também no exemplo de produção da documentação (`samples/doc-logging.md:142-144`), mas a semântica da chave **não é definida nos arquivos lidos**. O stack dá a cada canal a oportunidade de gravar; a decisão final depende do nível de severidade da mensagem (`samples/doc-logging.md:164`).

Níveis RFC 5424, do mais grave ao menos grave: **emergency, alert, critical, error, warning, notice, info, debug** (`samples/doc-logging.md:169`). A opção `level` é o mínimo para um canal gravar (`samples/doc-logging.md:169`); `Log::debug(...)` entra no `syslog` mas não no `slack` quando este exige `critical`, enquanto `Log::emergency(...)` entra em ambos (`samples/doc-logging.md:171-181`). Os oito métodos de escrita estão em `samples/doc-logging.md:188-199`, e o envio ao canal padrão em `samples/doc-logging.md:201`.

Exemplo de uso com placeholder (literal, `samples/doc-logging.md:219`):
```php
Log::info('Showing the user profile for user: {id}', ['id' => $id]);
```

## 1.4 Canais de arquivo

`single` (`samples/samples-config-logging.php:61-66`): `storage_path('logs/laravel.log')`, nível `env('LOG_LEVEL', 'debug')`, `replace_placeholders => true`.
`daily` (`samples/samples-config-logging.php:68-74`): mesmo caminho/nível, `max_files => env('LOG_DAILY_DAYS', 14)`.
`monthly` (`samples/samples-config-logging.php:76-82`): `max_files => 3`.

Opções adicionais dos três (`samples/doc-logging.md:80`): `bubble` (padrão `true`), `locking` (`false`), `permission` (`0644`) — tabela em `samples/doc-logging.md:84-88`. A retenção de `daily`/`monthly` é feita por `max_files`, com `LOG_DAILY_DAYS` aplicável ao `daily` (`samples/doc-logging.md:92`).

## 1.5 Canais de entrega externa/Syslog/Slack

`slack` (`samples/samples-config-logging.php:84-91`): `url` via `LOG_SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL`, `username` com fallback em `APP_NAME`/`Laravel`, `emoji` `:boom:`, `level => env('LOG_LEVEL', 'critical')`. Exige URL de incoming webhook (`samples/doc-logging.md:102`); por padrão só recebe `critical+`, ajustável por `LOG_LEVEL` ou pelo `level` do canal (`samples/doc-logging.md:104`).

`papertrail` (`samples/samples-config-logging.php:93-103`): driver `monolog`, `SyslogUdpHandler`, `handler_with` com `host`, `port` e `connectionString` TLS, mais `PsrLogMessageProcessor`. Requer `host`/`port`, normalmente `PAPERTRAIL_URL`/`PAPERTRAIL_PORT` (`samples/doc-logging.md:97`). `handler_with` fornece parâmetros construtores do handler (`samples/doc-logging.md:410`).

`stderr` (`samples/samples-config-logging.php:105-114`): `StreamHandler` em `php://stderr`, `formatter` via `LOG_STDERR_FORMATTER`, `PsrLogMessageProcessor`. `syslog` (`samples/samples-config-logging.php:116-121`) usa `facility => env('LOG_SYSLOG_FACILITY', LOG_USER)`; `errorlog` (`samples/samples-config-logging.php:123-127`) usa o driver homônimo; `null` (`samples/samples-config-logging.php:129-132`) é `monolog` + `NullHandler`, sem `level` declarado. O canal `emergency` (`samples/samples-config-logging.php:134-136`) declara apenas `path`; o comportamento exato dessa forma abreviada **não verificado** nos documentos lidos.

Stacks sob demanda: `Log::channel('slack')->info(...)` e `Log::stack(['single', 'slack'])->info(...)` (`samples/doc-logging.md:315-327`); canais construídos em runtime com `Log::build([...])` (`samples/doc-logging.md:332-341`) e embutidos em stacks (`samples/doc-logging.md:343-354`).

## 1.6 Customização Monolog

Há três níveis, todos documentados:

1. **`tap` em canal existente** — a classe recebe o `Illuminate\Log\Logger` após a criação e só precisa de `__invoke` (`samples/doc-logging.md:364`, `samples/doc-logging.md:376`); classes são resolvidas pelo container, com injeção de dependências (`samples/doc-logging.md:402-403`). Configuração (`samples/doc-logging.md:367-373`):
```php
'single' => [
    'driver' => 'single',
    'tap' => [App\Logging\CustomizeFormatter::class],
    'path' => storage_path('logs/laravel.log'),
    'level' => env('LOG_LEVEL', 'debug'),
    'replace_placeholders' => true,
],
```
A implementação troca o formatador de cada handler (`samples/doc-logging.md:391-397`):
```php
public function __invoke(Logger $logger): void
{
    foreach ($logger->getHandlers() as $handler) {
        $handler->setFormatter(new LineFormatter(
            '[%datetime%] %channel%.%level_name%: %message% %context% %extra%'
        ));
    }
}
```
2. **driver `monolog`** — `handler` + `handler_with` (`samples/doc-logging.md:408-421`); formatador padrão `LineFormatter`, substituível por `formatter`/`formatter_with` (`samples/doc-logging.md:426-437`) ou `formatter => 'default'` quando o handler já fornece um (`samples/doc-logging.md:439-447`); `processors` aceita sintaxe simples ou `['processor' => ..., 'with' => [...]]` (`samples/doc-logging.md:452-474`).
3. **driver `custom`** — `via` aponta uma factory cujo `__invoke(array $config): Logger` recebe o array de configuração do canal e devolve o Monolog (`samples/doc-logging.md:479-509`).

## 1.7 Pail (o único mecanismo de "tail" coberto pelos arquivos lidos)

Instalação como dependência de desenvolvimento (`samples/doc-logging.md:526-530`): `composer require --dev laravel/pail`; **requer a extensão PCNTL** (`samples/doc-logging.md:523-524`). Uso: `php artisan pail` (`samples/doc-logging.md:535-539`), `-v` evita truncamento e `-vv` mostra stack traces (`samples/doc-logging.md:541-551`). Funciona com qualquer driver, citando Nightwatch, Sentry e Flare (`samples/doc-logging.md:516`). Filtros literais: `--filter="QueryException"` (`samples/doc-logging.md:561-564`), `--message="User created"` (`samples/doc-logging.md:570-573`), `--level=error` (`samples/doc-logging.md:579-582`), `--user=1` (`samples/doc-logging.md:588-591`).

# 2. Fluxo de exceções com `withExceptions`

## 2.1 O skeleton real

`samples/samples-bootstrap-app.php:17-21`:
```php
->withExceptions(function (Exceptions $exceptions): void {
    $exceptions->shouldRenderJsonWhen(
        fn (Request $request) => $request->is('api', 'api/*') || $request->expectsJson(),
    );
})->create();
```
Áncoras do arquivo: `Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))` com `web`, `commands` e `health: '/up'` (`samples/samples-bootstrap-app.php:8-13`); `withMiddleware` vazio (`samples/samples-bootstrap-app.php:14-16`); imports de `Exceptions`, `Middleware`, `Request` (`samples/samples-bootstrap-app.php:3-6`). O objeto entregue ao closure é `Illuminate\Foundation\Configuration\Exceptions` (`samples/doc-errors.md:18-20`). O exemplo da documentação para `shouldRenderJsonWhen` aceita `(Request $request, Throwable $e)` e testa `admin/*` (`samples/doc-logging.md` não; `samples/doc-errors.md:271-286`); o skeleton usa apenas `Request` e rotas `api`/`api/*` — assinatura reduzida é compatível com o tipo esperado, mas o exame da implementação interna **não verificado**.

## 2.2 Report

Relatório = gravar em log ou enviar a Nightwatch/Sentry/Flare; por padrão segue a configuração de logging (`samples/doc-errors.md:38`). `report` registra closure cujo tipo é inferido pelo type-hint (`samples/doc-errors.md:40`). Mesmo com callback customizado, o log padrão **ainda acontece**; `->stop()` ou `return false` interrompem a propagação (`samples/doc-errors.md:52-66`). Alternativa: método `report()` na própria exceção, com injeção de dependências (`samples/doc-errors.md:312`, `samples/doc-errors.md:379-380`); `return false` delega ao tratamento padrão (`samples/doc-errors.md:360-377`). Helper `report($e)` permite relatar sem renderizar página de erro (`samples/doc-errors.md:115-128`); `dontReportDuplicates()` evita duplicatas **para a mesma instância** (`samples/doc-errors.md:135-158`).

**Contexto de exceções.** Se disponível, o ID do usuário é adicionado automaticamente; `context()` em `withExceptions` define contexto global de todas as exceções (`samples/doc-errors.md:74-82`):
```php
->withExceptions(function (Exceptions $exceptions): void {
    $exceptions->context(fn () => [
        'foo' => 'bar',
    ]);
})
```
Contexto por exceção vem do método `context()` da classe (`samples/doc-errors.md:87-110`), com exemplo literal `return ['order_id' => $this->orderId];` (`samples/doc-errors.md:105-107`).

**Nível.** `level(PDOException::class, LogLevel::CRITICAL)` altera o nível de log daquele tipo, relevante porque o nível decide em quais canais a mensagem aparece (`samples/doc-errors.md:163-176`).

## 2.3 Supressão

`dontReport([...])` impede o report, **mas não a renderização customizada** (`samples/doc-errors.md:181-191`); a interface `ShouldntReport` tem o mesmo efeito (`samples/doc-errors.md:193-207`); `dontReportWhen(closure)` permite condição por motivo (`samples/doc-errors.md:209-221`). Internamente Laravel já ignora 404, 403 por origem e 419 por CSRF, e `stopIgnoring(HttpException::class)` reverte isso (`samples/doc-errors.md:223-231`).

## 2.4 Render, status HTTP e páginas

`render` recebe a exceção e `Request`, devolve `Illuminate\Http\Response`; sem retorno, vale o render padrão (`samples/doc-errors.md:236-251`). Status explícito em `response()->view('errors.invalid-order', status: 500)` (`samples/doc-errors.md:244-249`); JSON 404 condicionado a `api/*` (`samples/doc-errors.md:257-265`). A decisão HTML × JSON vem do `Accept`, e `shouldRenderJsonWhen` a substitui (`samples/doc-errors.md:271-286`). `respond` personaliza a resposta final já montada — exemplo literal para 419 em `samples/doc-errors.md:296-305`:
```php
$exceptions->respond(function (Response $response) {
    if ($response->getStatusCode() === 419) {
        return back()->with([
            'message' => 'The page expired, please try again.',
        ]);
    }

    return $response;
});
```
Exceções `renderable` podem retornar `false` para manter a resposta padrão de exceções Laravel/Symfony (`samples/doc-errors.md:343-358`).

**Páginas de erro.** `abort(404)` gera o `HttpException` (`samples/doc-errors.md:471-475`); `resources/views/errors/404.blade.php` é usado para todo 404, com `$exception` disponível na view (`samples/doc-errors.md:480-484`); templates padrão via `php artisan vendor:publish --tag=laravel-errors` (`samples/doc-errors.md:486-490`). Fallbacks `4xx.blade.php`/`5xx.blade.php` **não afetam** 401, 402, 403, 404, 419, 429, 500 e 503, que têm páginas internas dedicadas (`samples/doc-errors.md:493-497`).

Visibilidade: `debug` em `config/app.php` segue `APP_DEBUG`; em produção deve ser **sempre `false`**, sob risco de expor valores sensíveis (`samples/doc-errors.md:25-30`).

## 2.5 Throttling

`throttle` recebe closure que devolve `Lottery` ou `Limit` (`samples/doc-errors.md:385-398`): `Lottery::odds(1, 1000)` para amostragem aleatória; seletivo por classe (`samples/doc-errors.md:400-414`); `Limit::perMinute(300)` contra bursts de terceiros (`samples/doc-errors.md:416-430`); chave padrão = classe da exceção, personalizável com `->by($e->getMessage())` (`samples/doc-errors.md:432-446`); `match (true)` pode combinar `Limit::perMinute`, `Lottery::odds` e `Limit::none()` (`samples/doc-errors.md:448-466`).

# 3. Contexto estruturado

## 3.1 Captura, propagação e metadados

Finalidade: capturar/recuperar/compartilhar informação através de requests, jobs e comandos, incluindo-a nos logs para rastrear fluxos distribuídos (`samples/doc-context.md:18`). Middleware literal (`samples/doc-context.md:41-47`):
```php
public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next): Response
{
    Context::add('url', $request->url());
    Context::add('trace_id', Str::uuid()->toString());

    return $next($request);
}
```
Os valores viram **metadados separados** do contexto por chamada. Exemplo literal de saída (`samples/doc-context.md:54-60`):
```php
Log::info('User authenticated.', ['auth_id' => Auth::id()]);
```
```text
User authenticated. {"auth_id":27} {"url":"https://example.com/login","trace_id":"e04e1a11-e75c-4db3-b5b5-cfef4ef56697"}
```
No despacho de job, o contexto corrente é capturado no payload e reidratado na execução (`samples/doc-context.md:63-74`): o log do `ProcessPodcast::handle()` (`samples/doc-context.md:86-90`) contém `url` e `trace_id` da request original (`samples/doc-context.md:97-101`).

API de escrita: `add('key','value')` e `add([...])` (`samples/doc-context.md:108-123`); `add` sobrescreve, `addIf` não (`samples/doc-context.md:125-137`); `increment`/`decrement` com valor opcional (`samples/doc-context.md:139-147`); `when(condição, sim, não)` (`samples/doc-context.md:152-163`); `scope(callback, data:, hidden:)` restaura o estado ao final (`samples/doc-context.md:168-199`), com aviso de que **mutação de objetos dentro do closure vaza para fora** (`samples/doc-context.md:201-202`). Stacks com `push`, `get`, `stackContains` e `stackContains` por closure (`samples/doc-context.md:207-257`); captura de SQL/duração via `DB::listen` em `samples/doc-context.md:230-234`. Leitura: `get`, `only`, `except`, `pull`, `pop`, `remember`, `all` (`samples/doc-context.md:262-309`); `has`/`missing`, com `has === true` mesmo para valor `null` (`samples/doc-context.md:314-335`). Remoção: `forget('chave')` e `forget([...])` (`samples/doc-context.md:340-358`).

## 3.2 Hidden

Dados hidden **não são anexados aos logs** e não aparecem nos getters normais (`samples/doc-context.md:363`), com espelho completo das operações em `samples/doc-context.md:377-392` (`addHidden`, `addHiddenIf`, `pushHidden`, `getHidden`, `pullHidden`, `popHidden`, `onlyHidden`, `exceptHidden`, `allHidden`, `hasHidden`, `missingHidden`, `forgetHidden`). Exemplo literal (`samples/doc-context.md:368-375`):
```php
Context::addHidden('key', 'value');

Context::getHidden('key');
// 'value'

Context::get('key');
// null
```
É o mecanismo documentado para manter dado sensível fora dos logs (`samples/doc-context.md:363`); o样本 lido não traz política de retenção/redação de segredos além disso.

## 3.3 `Log::withContext` × `Context` × `Log::shareContext`

`Log::withContext` aplica contexto a **todas as entradas seguintes de um canal específico** (`samples/doc-logging.md:239`). Middleware literal com request ID e devolução do header (`samples/doc-logging.md:259-272`):
```php
public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next): Response
{
    $requestId = (string) Str::uuid();

    Log::withContext([
        'request-id' => $requestId
    ]);

    $response = $next($request);

    $response->headers->set('Request-Id', $requestId);

    return $response;
}
```
`Log::shareContext` propaga para **todos os canais criados e os criados posteriormente** (`samples/doc-logging.md:276`), com o mesmo padrão de middleware em `samples/doc-logging.md:296-306`. Para contexto em jobs processados na fila, a documentação aponta para job middleware (`samples/doc-logging.md:309-310`).

Relação prática `[derivado dos trechos citados]`: `Context` é incrementado por metadados globais e cruza a fronteira request→job (`samples/doc-context.md:51`, `samples/doc-context.md:74`); `Log::withContext` é escopo de canal (`samples/doc-logging.md:239`); `Log::shareContext` é escopo global de canais (`samples/doc-logging.md:276`). Correlação com `tenant`: **nenhum dos arquivos lidos menciona tenant**. Aplicação derivada, usando apenas APIs literais — `Context::add(['tenant_id' => ..., 'trace_id' => ...])` (`samples/doc-context.md:119-123`, `samples/doc-context.md:43-44`) e/ou `Log::withContext(['request-id' => ..., 'tenant_id' => ...])` (`samples/doc-logging.md:263-265`); dado sensível do tenant vai em `Context::addHidden` (`samples/doc-context.md:368`).

Hooks de ciclo de vida: `dehydrating` no `boot` do `AppServiceProvider` captura `app.locale` em hidden (`samples/doc-context.md:404-422`); **não usar a facade `Context` dentro do callback**, apenas o `Repository` recebido, para não alterar o contexto do processo corrente (`samples/doc-context.md:424-425`). Simetricamente, `hydrated` restaura o valor (`samples/doc-context.md:430-450`) com a mesma restrição (`samples/doc-context.md:452-453`).
